subject: Physics
scope_summary: Current Grade-9 Simple Machines spine covering effort/load tradeoffs, mechanical advantage, practical same-state load/effort measurement, and qualitative comparison of levers, pulleys and inclined planes. The package remains CANDIDATE and does not promote itself to curriculum authority.

resources.section: Simple machines, mechanical advantage and lever practical
resources.rights_status: Author-created project draft; curriculum placement researched separately, no external scientific-review authority claimed.
resources.selection_reason: Provides self-contained Grade9V3 teaching for the currently verified Grade-9 simple-machines competency while keeping exact curriculum authority outside the authored package.

buckets.title: Simple machines
buckets.badge_reason: The arithmetic is simple; the durable difficulty is identifying effort/load sides, computing mechanical advantage from the same machine state, and explaining force/distance/direction tradeoffs without implying energy creation.

conventions.statement: Name the effort/input side and load/output side before comparing force or distance.

scope.covers: Grade-9 simple machines: identify pulley, inclined-plane and lever setups; define and calculate mechanical advantage; demonstrate/explain mechanical advantage from same-state load and effort measurements; connect force advantage to an ideal force-distance tradeoff.
excluded: Torque/moment equations as a required Grade-9 route.
Efficiency formulae or velocity-ratio catalogues beyond explicit later demand.

capabilities.action: Explain how a simple machine trades effort force, direction or input distance without creating energy.
capabilities.success_criterion: Rejects free-energy interpretations and identifies the compensating distance/direction tradeoff.

capabilities.action: Define, calculate and demonstrate mechanical advantage as load force divided by effort force using measurements from the same machine state.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses load and effort from the same steady machine state, calculates the dimensionless ratio MA = F_load/F_effort, and interprets MA greater than one as force advantage rather than energy creation or efficiency.

capabilities.action: Compare levers, pulleys and inclined planes by what they change about force, direction and input distance.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identifies lever, pulley and inclined-plane input/output roles and their qualitative force/direction/distance tradeoff without assuming that every machine reduces effort force.

microtopics.title: A machine trades force or direction for distance; it does not create work
microtopics.badge_reason: A larger output force looks like an energy gain unless input distance is tracked.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish force from work and identify work as a force acting through displacement.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A simple machine can reduce effort force or change its direction by requiring a different input distance; in the ideal model input work equals useful output work.

teaching_path.action: Name the effort point, load point, effort force, load force, effort distance and load distance.
teaching_path.why_valid: Force advantage cannot be interpreted without identifying both input and output sides.
teaching_path.output: input: F_effort, d_effort; output: F_load, d_load.

teaching_path.action: For an ideal machine, compare the effort and load work using F_effort d_effort = F_load d_load.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-IDEAL-MACHINE-WORK owns the lossless input-output work equality.
teaching_path.output: F_effort d_effort = F_load d_load; if F_effort < F_load for the same ideal output work, then d_effort > d_load.

teaching_path.action: Double the load force advantage while keeping ideal useful output work fixed and ask what must happen to effort distance.
teaching_path.why_valid: The boundary exposes why force multiplication does not create energy.
teaching_path.output: greater force advantage -> compensating greater input distance in the ideal tradeoff.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If a machine gives a larger output force than the effort force, it creates energy.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: An ideal machine doubles the output force. Can the effort point move the same distance as the load and still conserve work?
misconceptions.repair: Track both force and distance. In an ideal machine, a force advantage requires a compensating distance tradeoff.

exit_task.prompt: An ideal machine lets a person use a smaller effort force to raise a load. Without numbers, what must happen to the effort distance relative to the load distance if useful output work is unchanged?

answer.summary: The effort point must move farther than the load point when the effort force is smaller than the load force.
reasoning: Ideal input work equals useful output work.
Reducing input force while keeping output work fixed requires a larger input distance.
The machine trades force for distance rather than creating energy.
answer.check: If both force and distance were multiplied at the output with no extra input, output work would exceed input work and violate the ideal model.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit makes a qualitative ideal-work tradeoff claim without a computed value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created simple-machine work-tradeoff construction bound to the gate-owned ideal machine relation.

predict.prompt: Can an ideal machine make the load force larger than the effort force without any other tradeoff?
predict.defensible_answer: No. A force advantage requires a distance or direction tradeoff; ideal work is not created.

rubric.evidence_of: Treating machine benefit as a tradeoff rather than free energy.

rubric.criterion: Keeps ideal input and useful output work equal.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the energy account inherited from Work/Energy.

accepted: Smaller effort force requires a longer effort distance for the same ideal output work.
rejected: The machine makes extra work because the load force is larger.

route.ask: Which quantities determine work on each side?
What does the ideal model conserve?
If output force rises, what compensating quantity must change?

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path labels both sides first; the learner route begins from the apparent force gain and reconstructs the missing distance tradeoff.

boundary_test.prompt: If an ideal fixed pulley changes only the force direction, must it provide a force advantage greater than one?
boundary_test.answer: No. Changing direction alone can be useful even without reducing the effort-force magnitude.
boundary_test.confirms: Machine usefulness is not identical to force multiplication.

microtopics.title: Mechanical advantage is a same-state load-to-effort force ratio
microtopics.badge_reason: The ratio is simple; the fragile part is pairing load and effort from the same steady setup and not confusing force advantage with efficiency.
entry_assumptions: Can label input/effort and output/load forces on the same machine state.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Mechanical advantage is the dimensionless same-state force ratio MA = F_load/F_effort; a practical demonstration must measure both forces for one steady setup before forming the ratio, and the result says nothing by itself about efficiency.

teaching_path.action: Label the effort force and load force for one steady machine state before taking or using readings.
teaching_path.why_valid: Mechanical advantage compares simultaneous input/output force magnitudes for the same setup; mixing states makes the ratio physically meaningless.
teaching_path.output: one machine state with F_load and F_effort identified

teaching_path.action: Calculate MA = F_load/F_effort from those same-state force magnitudes.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-MECHANICAL-ADVANTAGE owns the dimensionless load-to-effort ratio.

teaching_path.action: Check that the force units cancel and interpret MA = 1 and MA > 1 without making an efficiency claim.
teaching_path.why_valid: Both quantities are forces, so MA is dimensionless; its meaning is force advantage only.
teaching_path.output: MA dimensionless; MA = 1 means equal load/effort magnitudes; MA > 1 means force advantage

teaching_path.action: For a lever demonstration, measure load and effort for the same balanced or steady setting, then repeat under a controlled setup change while keeping the load and measurement method fixed.
teaching_path.why_valid: A fair practical comparison changes the intended machine setup while preventing mixed-state or mixed-method readings from masquerading as a mechanical-advantage change.
teaching_path.output: same-state MA measurement plus one controlled comparison

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Mechanical advantage is the same as efficiency.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can an ideal fixed pulley have MA = 1 and still be useful?
misconceptions.repair: Yes. MA compares forces only; a machine can be useful by changing force direction even with MA = 1.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A load reading from one lever setting can be divided by an effort reading from a different setting to calculate mechanical advantage.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the effort point is moved between two lever settings, may you combine the old load reading with the new effort reading to form one MA?
misconceptions.repair: No. Measure load and effort for the same steady setting, then calculate MA for that state. Compare separate same-state ratios across controlled settings.

exit_task.prompt: A machine lifts a 120 N load with a 40 N effort. Find the mechanical advantage and interpret it.

answer.summary: MA = 3. The load force is three times the effort force.
reasoning: The ratio describes force advantage, not energy creation or efficiency.
answer.check: The newton units cancel, so MA is dimensionless.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created Grade9V3 mechanical-advantage construction aligned to the current Grade-9 competency and practical demand; no external package is treated as runtime authority.

predict.prompt: If a 120 N load is lifted with a 40 N effort, is the mechanical advantage less than, equal to, or greater than one?
predict.defensible_answer: Greater than one, because the load force is larger than the effort force.

attempt.produces: A same-state load/effort ratio with units cancelled, an interpretation, and a short lever-practical measurement plan.

rubric.criterion: Uses load divided by effort from the same machine state.
rubric.evidence_of: Maintaining both the MA convention and measurement custody.

rubric.criterion: Interprets the ratio as force advantage only.
rubric.evidence_of: Not confusing MA with efficiency or energy gain.
Keeping load and measurement method fixed while changing only the intended setup variable.

accepted: Same steady setting: MA = F_load/F_effort; units cancel. For a lever comparison, keep the load and measurement method fixed while changing only the intended lever setup feature.
rejected: Mix load and effort readings from different settings, or report MA in newtons.

route.ask: Which force belongs in the numerator?
Do the force units survive the division?
What does MA > 1 say, and what does it not say?
route.why_this_ask: It separates force advantage from efficiency.

route.ask: In a lever practical, which readings must come from the same setting before you form the ratio?
route.why_this_ask: It protects the experimental meaning of mechanical advantage.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path labels before dividing; the learner route begins from the meaning of a force advantage and reconstructs the ratio order.

boundary_test.prompt: What does MA = 1 mean about the load and effort force magnitudes?
boundary_test.answer: They are equal in magnitude; the machine provides no force multiplication.
boundary_test.confirms: Mechanical advantage is specifically a force ratio.

microtopics.title: Levers, pulleys and inclined planes realize different force-distance tradeoffs
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners can memorize device names without identifying what each machine changes about force, direction and distance.
entry_assumptions: Can explain the ideal force-distance tradeoff and compute mechanical advantage.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A lever, pulley or inclined plane should be analysed by its input/output force, direction and distance tradeoff rather than by a memorized claim that every simple machine reduces force.

teaching_path.action: For each machine, identify the effort point/direction and the load motion.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same input-output language lets different machine types be compared without separate memorized rules.
teaching_path.output: lever, pulley and ramp each have named effort and load sides.

teaching_path.action: Compare whether the machine mainly changes force magnitude, force direction, or required input distance in the stated setup.
teaching_path.why_valid: Simple-machine benefit is a geometric/input-output tradeoff, not a universal force reduction.
teaching_path.output: fixed pulley may change direction; force-advantage setups require extra input distance; incline spreads a height gain over a longer path.

teaching_path.action: Use an ideal fixed pulley as the counterexample to 'all machines reduce effort force'.
teaching_path.why_valid: A direction-changing machine can be useful with no force multiplication.
teaching_path.output: machine usefulness can be directional even when MA = 1.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every pulley, lever or inclined plane must reduce the effort force.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What useful change can an ideal fixed pulley provide even when effort and load force magnitudes are equal?
misconceptions.repair: It can reverse the direction of the required effort. Identify the actual setup before claiming force advantage.

exit_task.prompt: Compare an ideal fixed pulley with a long inclined plane used to raise the same load. State one useful change each machine can provide without claiming that either creates energy.

answer.summary: The fixed pulley can change the effort direction; the inclined plane can reduce the required force by spreading the same height gain over a longer input path.
reasoning: The fixed pulley can redirect the pull even when force magnitude is not reduced.
The incline increases the distance over which the load reaches the same height.
Both are input-output tradeoffs consistent with work conservation in the ideal model.
answer.check: Neither description requires useful output work to exceed ideal input work.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit compares qualitative machine functions without a calculated device-specific force formula.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created cross-machine comparison using the shared work ledger.

predict.prompt: If a fixed pulley does not reduce force magnitude, can it still count as a useful simple machine?
predict.defensible_answer: Yes. It can change the direction in which the effort force is applied.

attempt.produces: One input-output tradeoff for a pulley, lever or incline.

rubric.evidence_of: Comparing machines by function rather than name.

accepted: Fixed pulley: direction change; incline: smaller force over longer path.
rejected: Every simple machine always multiplies force.

route.ask: What motion must the load complete?
Which quantity changes most clearly: force, direction or distance?
Does a fixed pulley falsify 'all machines reduce force'?

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path compares named machines in one framework; the learner route begins from a specific setup and reconstructs the functional category.

boundary_test.prompt: Can a machine be useful if its mechanical advantage is exactly one?
boundary_test.answer: Yes. It can still change force direction or make the task ergonomically easier.
boundary_test.confirms: Mechanical advantage is not the only form of machine usefulness.

relations.meaning: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of load force magnitude to effort force magnitude.
conditions: Load and effort magnitudes refer to the same machine state.

derivation.action: Divide load-force magnitude by effort-force magnitude.
derivation.why_valid: The gate defines mechanical advantage as this force ratio.

limits: Mechanical advantage alone does not measure efficiency or energy loss.
checks: MA = 1 means equal load and effort force magnitudes.

relations.meaning: For an ideal lossless simple machine, input work equals useful output work.
conditions: Each force magnitude is paired with displacement along its own line of action.

derivation.action: Equate ideal input work and useful output work.
derivation.why_valid: The ideal machine transfers work without loss rather than creating it.

limits: Real machines can require more input work because of losses.
checks: A force advantage greater than one requires a corresponding distance disadvantage in the ideal model.

question_families.title: Grade 9 simple-machine tradeoff practice
solution_structure: Identify whether force magnitude, direction or distance is changing.
Use mechanical advantage or the ideal work tradeoff only after the setup is identified.
Check that no energy is created.

demand_dimensions.model_choice: Decide whether a force ratio or qualitative work tradeoff is the relevant model.
demand_dimensions.representation_translation: Translate a machine sketch or description into effort/load sides without relying on device name alone.
demand_dimensions.reasoning_steps: Carry input/output labels through the force-distance tradeoff and energy check.
demand_dimensions.novelty: Map an unfamiliar tool onto lever, pulley or inclined-plane input/output reasoning.

safe_variations: Change load/effort values, machine orientation or everyday context while keeping the same ideal tradeoff.
transfer_boundaries: Do not infer device-specific force formulae that the gate registry has not declared.
common_wrong_routes: Treating force multiplication as energy multiplication.
Assuming every simple machine reduces effort force.

questions.stem: A simple machine supports a 150 N load with a 50 N effort. Find the mechanical advantage and state what that number does not tell you.

answer.summary: MA = 3. It tells you the force ratio, not the efficiency or whether the machine creates energy.
reasoning: Efficiency and energy loss require additional information.
answer.check: A mechanical advantage of 3 can coexist with different efficiencies in different real machines.

hints.text: Put the load force in the numerator and effort force in the denominator.

questions.stem: Plan a lever experiment to calculate mechanical advantage. State how you measure load and effort for one balanced/steady lever setting, how you calculate M.A., and one control needed for a fair comparison across settings.
conditions: Use force magnitudes measured for the same lever setting.

answer.summary: Measure the load-force magnitude and the effort-force magnitude for the same steady lever state, calculate M.A. = Load/Effort, repeat for controlled settings, and keep the load and measurement method consistent when comparing how the setup changes the required effort.
reasoning: Identify the load side and effort side before taking readings.
Use force readings from the same steady/balanced lever state.
For comparisons, keep the load and measuring instruments/method consistent while changing only the intended lever setup variable.
Repeat readings to reduce the influence of random measurement error.
answer.check: A load reading from one setting divided by an effort reading from a different setting is not a valid mechanical-advantage measurement.

hints.text: Load and effort must be measured for the same lever setting before forming the ratio.
For a fair comparison, keep the load fixed while changing only the intended setup feature.
